items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: And I'm, I really like to, like to feel as though I'm, I'm, I'm being influenced by, by him right now.

ctx.x: When I hear your piano, that's what I think of Earl Hines more than.

Earl Hines, and you mentioned one of your favorites was Jess Stacy, who also was one of my favorites. And then I had so many, like Joe Sullivan, you know, and Bob Surkey, and oh, I can't hear that. You had an avalanche of great pianists, you know. I mean, so many, so many good ones. And they all were a little bit different styles, you know. Well, who's influenced your style the most? Or do you see yourself as having a certain style? I have to say now that, that in later years, in later years, I've turned more,…
Uh-huh. That's the only way I can put it. Uh-huh. Well, can, maybe, do, do we have enough tape there to, for Arvin to play something now, or is he gonna?

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: I think, I think Jelly Roll did a lot of, a lot of standout work on the piano too.

ctx.x: Yeah, that's right. That's right. It was more or less, uh, if you got a good banjo player, and a good drummer, uh, all, all you'd have to do was just, just work right along with that piano, work right along with that, that, that, with that octave in the bass, or a single note, as I said before, and with a, a chord in the right hand, using mostly a tonic. Because, in those days, we didn't use any fancy chords. We didn't use any of those flatted fifths, and those progressive harmonies that they use in the day. We…
I wanted to ask you something about that trumpet player that was playing in front of you, Bill Gillan? Bill Gillan?

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1965-09-13
items.q: I was already going under the influence of the old timers like Jelly Roll and the ragtime pianists.

ctx.x: You said before that there were no specific pianists who influenced you when you came up. Generally speaking, what pianists would influence your style, do you think?

Well, I heard pianists all around me, but many of the good pianists, such as Jelly Roll, had already gone. As you say, why did some of these musicians hate to leave? Well, they all hated to leave, I guess, but more or less the musicians who felt that they wanted to make something, or make a name, or make money, they couldn't do it in the Walls. They had to leave. And, of course, Jelly Roll was gone, Spencer Williams was gone, Clarence Williams, King Oliver, all the real greats struck out sooner or later. And…
Well, certainly your piano style goes beyond the ragtime realm. What have any other pianists of the swing era or the modern era influence your playing as it's constituted today?
